accuracy.evidence: Checked against the DfE EYFS Statutory Framework ELG Number ('subitise (recognise quantities without counting) up to 5'), Development Matters 3 and 4 year olds ('Fast recognition of up to 3 objects, without having to count them individually (subitising)'), and Clements and Sarama on perceptual subitising (about 1 to 4 items). Dice patterns use the standard pip layouts: 1 centre, 2 diagonal, 3 slant.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented early-number errors: non-conservation of number (Piaget's row task: spreading out seems to make more), judging quantity by size or area, treating an empty set as 'one', and showing all five fingers for any number. Each appears in a prediction, the lab feedback and the challenge.

lab_distinct.evidence: The flash plate hides dots after 1.1 s so counting is not possible, which is the defining mechanism of subitising; the spread mat tests conservation by direct dragging; the dice to birds match shows one number in two arrangements; the tappable hand maps a group to raised fingers. No other flagship lab times a covered display or uses a finger hand.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child first succeeds at quick looks (three right answers needed), then discovers that moving dots does not change the amount, then sees the same number as a line of birds and a slanted dice face, then expresses a quantity with fingers, and finally separates how many from how big. Each step's confirm text names the idea after the child has done it.

predictions.evidence: Two locked predictions with tempting wrong options: 'If the 3 dots go far apart, how many? More than 3' (the mat keeps showing Still 3) and '2 big balls or 3 tiny beads, which has more? The big balls' (the basket sort accepts only how many, with a size-specific message).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating challenge questions with twelve distinct m= wrong-answer messages: one fewer and one more for the triangle, spreading adds none, none went away, bigger but fewer, 2 is not 3, too many and too few birds for the dice, empty plate is none (two versions), all five fingers is 5, and one finger too many.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use one-syllable words and sentences of two to eight words (Look fast! One dot. Still three!) for read-aloud at 3 to 4; adult text stays under the family limit while naming subitising, cardinality and conservation of number. Canvas prompts are under eight words and the young class gives large tap targets.

no_filler.evidence: Passes the filler regex and the 12% duplicate gate. Every kid paragraph carries one idea (quick look, arrangements, spreading out, size), every adult paragraph has one job (term and curriculum aim, cardinality and varied patterns, mistakes, what the lab does), and the family tip is a concrete raisin game.

mobile.evidence: Walkthrough passes on iPhone 13 (390 px). Number tiles, dice, fingers and baskets are spaced by width so none overlap at 390 px, text uses maxWidth so nothing clips, and every action has a full-width button in the control row under the canvas.

accessibility.evidence: Every drag and tap has a button twin (Peek, 1 2 3, Spread out, Bunch up, dice and fence buttons, One more or One less finger, baskets). The canvas aria-label is rewritten after every action with the current state, for example 'Fence A has 2 birds' and fingers up. axe WCAG 2.1 AA is clean in both themes in the walkthrough.
